analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from regulating carbon dioxide until China, India, and Russia cut theirs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or a vote when Congress ended January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the EPA and every other federal agency from regulating carbon dioxide until the Commerce Department certified in writing that China, India, and Russia had begun cutting emissions in ways "substantially similar" to what the United States proposed. Because that certification depended on decisions by three foreign governments, the ban would likely have lasted indefinitely. It never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-fired power plants, refineries, mines, and other large emitters, which would avoid the cost of federal carbon rules — retrofits, cleaner fuels, emissions permits — for as long as the foreign-certification condition held. Households might see marginally lower energy prices in the short run, though most of the avoided cost would stay with the industry.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal, oil, gas, and large emitters

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA and the head of every other federal agency from regulating carbon dioxide emissions.
Lifts the ban only after the Secretary of Commerce certifies in writing that China, India, and Russia have begun reductions "substantially similar" to those proposed for the United States.
Power plants, refineries, and other large emitters would avoid federal carbon compliance costs for as long as that certification was never issued.

analysis.who_pays: The public: carbon dioxide would keep flowing without federal limits, so the health and climate costs of those emissions land on everyone. Rules tied to carbon limits that also saved consumers money — such as vehicle standards — would be blocked too, while any energy-bill savings would be modest and uncertain.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The off-switch sits with three foreign governments: no U.S. official could control when — or whether — China, India, and Russia adopted "substantially similar" cuts, so the ban was effectively indefinite.

Blocking all federal carbon regulation would have stopped rules being phased in for vehicles and power plants, rules whose benefits include less fuel burned and fewer conventional pollutants in the air.
Any short-term savings on energy bills would be small and uncertain, while the deferred costs — climate damage and air-pollution health effects — accumulate for decades.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow almost entirely to large emitters, with only modest and speculative pass-through to consumers. Against that, the bill would have traded away U.S. authority over its own emissions for a certification about foreign action that might never come. The honest argument behind it — that one country's cuts cannot fix a global problem — is a real debate about climate policy, but this bill answered it by switching off American rules rather than by shaping international agreements.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with no cosponsors on August 4, 2010 and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on August 4, 2010; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
Not one senator joined as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote ever appeared in the bill's history.
The bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, leaving the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide intact.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the EPA carbon rules this bill would have switched off, and industries betting on cleaner energy kept the regulatory direction the bill threatened. The large emitters the bill was written to shield gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people — EPA carbon authority stayed intact

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 4, 2010 and recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Zero senators from either party signed on and the bill never reached a vote, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: Coal plants are among the largest U.S. carbon dioxide sources; the ban would spare them retrofit and closure costs from EPA rules, while the public absorbs the pollution and climate damage instead.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refineries and vehicle emissions were moving under EPA carbon regulation; the bill lifts that burden from the industry while drivers and communities downwind carry the cost of the emissions.
Industrial facilities faced carbon permitting as federal rules phased in; the bill cancels those compliance costs, with the emissions bill left to the public.

With federal carbon limits switched off indefinitely, the policy pressure driving demand for wind, solar, and efficiency work disappears — a loss for those firms that runs alongside the public's loss.
